subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
The big idea of this unit is joyful: we can make our own little games, and then we try them to see if they work. But the real computing lesson is not “make a big game”. It is three tiny skills, taught one at a time, in the happy context of making games. Second, you learn to find an error — to spot where the blocks do not match their plan. Third, you learn to debug — to fix the wrong block so the game works. These three skills are the whole unit.

The star word of this unit is testing — simply trying your program to see if it works. If it does what we wanted, it works. If it does the wrong thing, we have found an error, and fixing that error is called debugging. Mistakes are completely normal — even the grown-ups who make the biggest games test them over and over to find and fix errors.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 1 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Say what a games developer is — a person who makes computer games — and feel like one.
In ScratchJr, add a character and join a few picture blocks to make a tiny game.
Use the Start on Tap block so the character does something when it is tapped.
Run and test a program — try it (for a tap game, tap the character) and check it does what they wanted.
Understand that testing means trying your program to see if it works.
Predict what a short program will do, then test it to find out.
Find an error — spot the one block that does not match the plan (a wrong number, direction, or start block).
Know that fixing an error is called debugging, and debug a short program by changing one block and testing again.
Stay cheerful about mistakes and keep trying — the heart of being a games developer.

toolkit.name: ScratchJr
steps: Open ScratchJr on a tablet.
Tap the house, then tap the plus to start a new project.
Drag the coloured picture blocks together to make your character move.
Tap the green flag to run it.

concepts.title: We are games developers! (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
A games developer is a person who makes computer games. Today we become games developers. A game has a character (like a frog) and blocks that tell it what to do. Some games do something when you tap them.

Who has played a game on a tablet or a phone? What did you do — did you tap the screen? Did you make something jump? The people who make those games have a special name. They are called games developers.
concepts.example: And today — we are games developers! Start with games you already love.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you put the three blocks in a sensible order — a start block first and End last?

concepts.title: Make a tap game and test it (ScratchJr)
concepts.explanation:
Today we open ScratchJr and make the frog hop when we tap it. Then we test it — we try it to check that it works. The star word is testing: trying your program to see if it works. Teach the magic habit: make it, then try it.

The yellow block starts things. The blue block makes our frog hop.
concepts.example: Show ScratchJr on a big screen so everyone can see. Open a new project, tap the picture button to choose a Background, then tap the blue plus to add a character — a frog.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you join the three blocks and tap to test? Can you add a background and a character?

concepts.title: Find the error (ScratchJr and paper)
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes we test our game and it does the wrong thing. That is an error — a mistake. We find the error by looking at our plan, then at our blocks, and spotting where they do not match.

Maya wanted her cat to move just 1 step. She tested it — but the cat zoomed 3 steps too far! Something is wrong.
concepts.example: That is an error. Let us find it.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you compare the plan to the blocks and point to the block that does not match?

concepts.title: Debug it: fix the mistake (ScratchJr)
concepts.explanation:
When we find an error, we fix it. Finding a mistake and fixing it is called debugging. We change the one wrong block for the right one, then we test again. Everyone makes errors — even the people who make your favourite games — so an error is nothing to worry about. It is just a little puzzle to solve.

Sami made a frog game. He taps the frog. but nothing happens! Poor Sami.
concepts.example: Let us debug it — let us find the mistake and fix it. Show the classic tap bug.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you test again after fixing? Can you stay cheerful and treat the bug as a puzzle, not a disaster? Can you find the one wrong block and say what it should be?

concepts.title: Make your own tap game: the Mini-Project
concepts.explanation:
You choose a character, plan what it will do when tapped, build it in ScratchJr, test it, then find and fix a bug. This session and the Mini-Project sheet go hand in hand.

Today you are a real games developer. Choose your character. What will it do when you tap it — hop? move? say a word?
concepts.example: Let us plan it, build it, test it, and fix it. Show the Mini-Project sheet.
concepts.checkYourself: Does the game do the right thing when tapped — did you test it? Did you find and fix the bug? Did you keep trying with a smile? Does you plan before building?

frog cat dog bird

activities.materials: The printed activity page (or a sheet of paper), a pencil and colours
steps: We want the frog to hop when we tap it. Write 1, 2, 3 in the boxes to put the blocks in order.
[ ] Hop
[ ] Start on Tap

Think: which block goes first? Which one goes last?

activities.title: Make It Hop When You Tap!
activities.materials: The printed activity page (or a sheet of paper), a pencil and colours
steps: Add a frog. Join these blocks. Then tap the frog to test it!
Hop 4
Did the frog hop when you tapped it? Yes / Not yet
Now change the 4 to a bigger number. Tap the frog again. Did it hop higher? Yes / No
Trying your game to see if it works is called testing. Well done — you tested your game!

activities.title: Find the Error
activities.materials: The printed activity page (or a sheet of paper), a pencil and colours
steps: Maya wanted her cat to move 1 step. She tested it — but the cat went too far! One block is wrong. That is an error. Circle the wrong block.
The cat should MOVE 1 step right.
What number should it be? Move ______ step right.

activities.title: Fix the Bug
activities.materials: The printed activity page (or a sheet of paper), a pencil and colours
steps: Sami tapped his frog, but nothing happened! A mistake in a game is a bug. Circle the block that is wrong.
Hop 4
Which block should it be instead? Start on ______________.
Tip: for a tap game, we need the block that waits for a tap. Fixing it is called debugging!

activities.title: Draw
activities.materials: The printed activity page (or a sheet of paper), a pencil and colours
steps: You are a games developer! Draw your character doing something fun.
Did You Know?
One of the very first computer games ever made was called Pong. It was like table tennis — just two little lines and a dot that went beep!

Every games developer tests their game lots and lots of times. Even the people who make the biggest games play them over and over to find and fix mistakes. So you are working just like a real games developer!

debugging.symptom: If I made it, it must work.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Not always! That is exactly why we test — we try it to check. Even the people who make the biggest games test them again and again.

debugging.symptom: A mistake means I am bad at this.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Not at all. Everyone makes errors, even grown-ups who build computer games. Finding and fixing an error is what a games developer does all day.

debugging.symptom: The computer will fix it by itself.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: It will not. The computer does exactly what the blocks say, even when they are wrong. We have to find the wrong block and change it ourselves.

debugging.symptom: Start on Tap and Start on Green Flag are the same.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: They start the game in different ways. In a tap game, the wrong one means tapping does nothing. Start on Tap waits for you to tap the character; Start on Green Flag waits for the green flag at the top.

debugging.symptom: I must change lots of blocks to fix it.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: Usually just one block is wrong. Find that one block, change it, then test. Change one thing at a time.

debugging.symptom: Testing is only at the very end.
debugging.cause: A common misunderstanding about this idea.
debugging.fix: No — we test all the time, after every little change. That is how a games developer catches errors early, while they are still easy to find.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in debug it: fix the mistake (scratchjr), and give one example of your own.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
When we find an error, we fix it. Finding a mistake and fixing it is called debugging. We change the one wrong block for the right one, then we test again. Everyone makes errors — even the people who make your favourite games — so an error is nothing to worry about. It is just a little puzzle to solve.

Sami made a frog game. He taps the frog. but nothing happens! Poor Sami.

project.title: Unit 9 Project: Be a Games Developer
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Games Developer into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a games developer project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I built my tap game in ScratchJr.
I tapped my character to test it.
I found and fixed the bug.
I added one thing to make it better.

selfAssessment: I can say what a games developer is — a person who makes computer games — and feel like one.
I can in ScratchJr, add a character and join a few picture blocks to make a tiny game.
I can use the Start on Tap block so the character does something when it is tapped.
I can run and test a program — try it (for a tap game, tap the character) and check it does what they wanted.
I can understand that testing means trying your program to see if it works.
I can predict what a short program will do, then test it to find out.
I can find an error — spot the one block that does not match the plan (a wrong number, direction, or start block).
I can know that fixing an error is called debugging, and debug a short program by changing one block and testing again.
I can stay cheerful about mistakes and keep trying — the heart of being a games developer.
